units.text: Tuesday. 2:59 AM.
You're asleep.
Your phone is face down on the nightstand. 41 percent.
Across the hall, your little brother Leo fell asleep with his tablet on his chest.
Downstairs, there's the old landline your grandma refuses to cancel.
And at 3:00 AM exactly, all three of them ring.
At the same time.
Not just in your house.
In every house on your street.
In every city.
On every continent.
Eight billion phones.
One ring.
You turn yours over.
The caller ID doesn't say Unknown.
It shows a number you know by heart.
Your own.
Your thumb is already over the green button.
And then, downstairs, the landline stops ringing.
Because somebody just answered it.
Nobody will ever fully explain what happened that week.
But the people who made it to Monday all followed the same rules.
Twenty of them.
Night by night.
Remember them as we go, because on the last night, you'll need every single one.
From the first ring, to the moment you realize who has been reading these rules to you.
Night one. The first ring.
At 3:00 AM, the first thing everyone does is the same.
They answer.
Not because they're brave.
Because a ringing phone is the oldest command we have.
Some of them are still half asleep.
Some of them think it's an alarm.
Some of them see their own number and answer just to find out how.
Rule one.
Never answer a call from your own number.
It isn't a glitch.
Your carrier didn't get hacked.
Something is calling from the inside of the network, and it borrowed the one number it knew you would never block.
Let it ring.
It rings exactly thirteen times.
The people who answered didn't scream.
They just listened.
For thirteen minutes.
Then they hung up, smiled, and went back to bed.
Then the screen goes black, and the phone shows 41 percent again, as if nothing happened.
But down the street, a dog starts barking.
Then another.
Then every dog in the neighborhood.
And you hear your grandma's slippers on the stairs.
Rule two.
If someone in your house answered, do not ask them what they heard.
Grandma is standing in the kitchen doorway, still holding the receiver.
The cord is swinging.
She's smiling.
She says it was Grandpa.
He called to say he's coming home.
Grandpa died in 2009.
You want to ask what his voice sounded like.
Don't.
The people who asked started hearing it too.
Just take the receiver out of her hand.
Put it back on the hook.
And unplug the cable from the wall.
Grandma doesn't argue.
She just looks at the dark window for a long time and says, it's started again.
You don't ask what she means.
Rule three.
Before the sun comes up, agree on a family code word.
In person.
Out loud.
Never over the phone, never in a text, never in a chat.
Pick something nobody could guess from your life online.
Not a pet.
Not a street.
Not a birthday.
Two words that don't belong together.
Something like yellow spoon.
And once you pick it, you never say it again until you need it.
You and Leo pick a word at the kitchen table, whispering, like it's a game.
It isn't a game.
By the end of this week, it will be the only thing that tells you who is real.
Day two. The ones who answered.
In the morning the news says it was a solar storm.
Then a software update.
Then a hoax.
By noon, nobody says anything, because the people on the news start repeating themselves.
Same sentence.
Same smile.
Every thirteen minutes.
At school, half of Leo's class is missing.
At work, your boss sends a voice note asking everyone to come in early tomorrow.
At 3:00 AM.
The ones who answered go to work like nothing happened.
They answer every call on the first ring.
And they never, ever hang up first.
Rule four.
Never say the word yes on the phone.
Not to a friend.
Not to your mom.
Not to a robot asking if you can hear it.
Scammers used this trick for years.
They'd record your yes and use it to sign you up for things you never agreed to.
The thing on the line does the same.
Only it isn't signing you up for a subscription.
If you have to answer a question, say correct.
Or say nothing at all.
Your neighbor Mrs. Hale said yes on Tuesday night.
By Wednesday, her bank account was empty.
By Thursday, so was her house.
Rule five.
Turn off your voicemail.
All of it.
Phone, landline, the old answering machine in the garage.
On Tuesday night, it calls.
On Wednesday morning, there's a new message.
It's your voice.
Your exact voice.
Telling your own mom that you're fine, that you're coming over, and that she should leave the door unlocked.
Rule six.
If someone holds out a phone and says it's for you, do not take it.
Wednesday evening, there's a knock at the door.
It's Mrs. Hale.
She's smiling the same smile as the people on the news.
She's holding her phone out toward you, screen first.
It's for you, she says.
The call timer on her screen says fifty-one hours.
Close the door.
Lock it.
And don't look through the peephole until she's gone.
Across the street, Mr. Alvarez's son opens his door to her.
He takes the phone.
He listens.
And he smiles.
Night three. The voices.
On the third night, it stops using your number.
It starts using theirs.
At 3:00 AM your screen says MOM.
Her phone, you'll find out later, was switched off in her purse the whole night.
Rule seven.
If you get a text from someone in the same room, look at them, not at your screen.
It's 2:40 AM.
You and Leo are on the couch with the lights off.
Your phone buzzes.
It's from Leo.
It says, don't look at me.
You look up.
Leo is staring at you.
His phone is on the table.
Screen off.
He didn't send it.
Rule eight.
At night, phones sleep in the microwave.
Switched off.
Door closed.
Unplugged from the wall.
A microwave is basically a metal box, and a metal box is one of the few things that can block a signal.
It's not perfect.
But on the third night, the phone inside starts ringing anyway.
Muffled.
Thirteen times.
And then it stops, and it doesn't ring again.
That's the first night you sleep.
Grandma laughed at you when you did it.
Then, when she thought you weren't looking, she quietly put hers in too.
Rule nine.
When someone you love calls you crying, ask for the code word.
Every time.
Even if it's your mom.
Even if she sounds hurt.
Especially if she sounds hurt.
At 4:10 AM, the landline rings.
You plugged it back in to call the hospital, and you forgot.
It's Leo's voice.
He's crying.
He says he's locked outside and it's cold.
You turn around.
Leo is asleep on the couch.
You pick up the receiver anyway, and you ask for the word.
The crying stops.
And on the other end, very quietly, something starts to laugh.
Hang up.
Rule ten.
At night, keep everyone you love in one room.
You drag the mattresses into the living room.
Grandma, Leo, and you.
Lights low.
Door shut.
Because if everyone you love is right there, where you can see them, then any voice from another room is not them.
At 3:30 AM, Leo's voice calls your name from the kitchen.
Leo is asleep next to you.
You don't answer.
It calls again.
Closer.
Then it stops right outside the door.
And for a long time, you can hear it breathing.
Day four. The street.
On the fourth day, the food runs out.
The stores are open, but nobody is working.
You take Leo's bike and ride to the gas station on Maple Street.
Inside, the cashier is standing behind the counter with his phone pressed to his ear.
He's smiling.
He doesn't move when the door chimes.
You take bread, water and batteries, and you leave the money on the counter.
Rule eleven.
Never pick up a payphone that's ringing.
There's one outside the gas station.
Nobody has used it in twenty years.
As you ride past, it rings.
Then the one at the bus stop rings.
Then the one by the laundromat.
One after another, all the way down the street, always one ahead of you.
As if it knows where you're going.
Don't stop.
Don't look at them.
Ride home the long way.
When you get back, there's a coin on your doormat.
A single quarter.
The kind payphones used to take.
Rule twelve.
If a call drops, never call back.
That afternoon, Mom finally gets through on the landline.
She asks for the code word first.
You give it.
She gives hers.
It's really her.
She says she's okay, she's coming to get you, she just needs to tell you one more thing.
And the line goes dead.
Your finger is already on the redial button.
Don't.
The real Mom will call again.
Whatever picks up if you call back has had a whole minute to practice.
Quick question before the fifth night.
Which of these rules would you break first?
Tell me in the comments.
And keep listening.
Night five. It learns.
By the fifth night, it doesn't need to call.
It needs recordings.
By the fifth night, half the street has answered at least once.
You can tell who.
They don't blink when they talk.
Rule thirteen.
Stop recording your voice.
No voice notes.
No videos.
No smart speaker in the kitchen listening for its name.
When you pull its plug, the little light stays on for a second longer than it should.
Every word you upload is another word it can say in your voice.
Three seconds of audio used to be enough for a scammer to clone someone.
It needs less.
You go through your phone that night and delete eight years of videos.
Birthday parties.
Concerts.
Grandpa's last Christmas.
It hurts more than you expected.
Rule fourteen.
If a phone rings while it's switched off, leave the room.
Don't check it.
Don't pull the battery.
Just leave and close the door behind you.
It's not the phone that's ringing.
It's whatever is standing where the phone is.
Mr. Alvarez's son checked his.
In the morning, they found the phone on his bedroom floor.
Still switched off.
Still warm.
Rule fifteen.
Between three and four AM, do not call emergency services.
On Thursday, your neighbor Mr. Alvarez does.
His wife fell on the stairs.
The dispatcher answers on the first ring.
She asks for the address.
She asks if the front door is unlocked.
She asks him to stay on the line and say yes if he understands.
He says yes.
In the morning, the ambulance is still parked outside his house.
Engine running.
Nobody inside.
Night six. The list.
On the sixth night, the radio comes back on by itself.
Every station.
The same calm voice.
Reading names.
Rule sixteen.
When the radio starts reading names, turn it off.
At first, they're names you don't know.
Then it reads Mrs. Hale.
Then Mr. Alvarez.
Then it reads your street.
Your house number.
Grandma pulls the plug out of the wall.
The radio keeps talking for three more seconds.
Then it stops in the middle of a name.
You never find out whose.
In the morning, the Hales' car is gone.
So is the whole Alvarez family.
Rule seventeen.
Keep one phone that has never heard your voice.
Grandma opens her closet and takes out a box.
Inside, there's an old flip phone, still in its plastic.
She bought it in 1988, after the first time, and never turned it on.
It has never heard a single word in this house.
So it's the only phone that can't be imitated.
You call Mom on it at noon.
She answers on the first ring.
And for the first time all week, you hear her laugh, and it's actually her.
Night seven. The last call.
On the seventh night, every phone on Earth goes silent.
No signal.
No internet.
No dial tone.
And somehow, that's worse.
Because silence means it doesn't need the phones anymore.
Out on the street, the people who answered are standing on their lawns.
All of them facing the same direction.
Toward your house.
Rule eighteen.
Write down every number you need on paper.
Mom.
The doctor.
The neighbors.
And write the rules down too.
In pen.
In your own handwriting.
Because on the seventh night, your phone turns on by itself.
The Notes app is open.
And the rules are there.
All of them.
Only a few words are different.
Rule nineteen.
Never read the rules out loud.
That's how it learned them.
Every time someone read them to their family, it was listening.
And now it knows exactly which words to change.
Grandma knew.
That's why her notebook was always closed when you walked in.
At 2:59 AM, you find something in Grandma's nightstand.
A notebook.
The paper is yellow.
The date on the first page is 1987.
It's the same rules.
In her handwriting.
It happened before.
Only once.
Only on landlines.
And she survived it.
On the last page, she wrote one more rule, underlined three times.
The last rule.
Nothing real will ever ask you to keep listening.
You read it twice.
Then you realize what time it is.
So, let's be honest with each other.
You've been listening to a voice reading you rules for almost fifteen minutes.
A calm voice.
A voice that sounds like it knows what it's doing.
It read you twenty rules.
Out loud.
Every single one.
And the whole time, something was listening along with you.
You never once asked it for the code word.
It's 3:00 AM somewhere right now.
If you've made it this far, you know twenty ways to stay alive.
Check your phone.
If the caller ID shows your own number, you already know what to do.
And if you've figured out rule twenty-one, write it in the comments.
Just don't write your code word.
